li.a: CNN: July 2, 2025, Sean "Diddy" Combs denied bail as he awaits sentencing
Reuters, published by Malay Mail: Jury clears Sean Combs of racketeering, convicts him on prostitution-related charges, bail denied
NPR: Why the Sean Combs trial is about more than "Diddy vs. Cassie"
Variety: Diddy sentenced to four years in prison
ABC7 New York: Federal appeals court to hear arguments about overturning Sean Combs' conviction
Law Commentary: Sean Combs appeals sentence as court weighs early release bid
LitigationLogic: Sean Combs appeals 50-month sentence at Second Circuit over acquitted conduct
WBLS: Diddy's release date moved up again

content.p: On 2 July 2025 a federal jury in Manhattan cleared the music executive Sean "Diddy" Combs of racketeering conspiracy and of two counts of sex trafficking, the charges that could have put him in prison for life, but convicted him on two counts of taking people across state lines to engage in prostitution, formally called transportation to engage in prostitution. Three months later Judge Arun Subramanian sentenced him to 50 months. He is serving that term at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey, and as of the latest reports a federal appeals court has yet to rule on his challenge to the sentence and conviction.

The split verdict has defined the case since. His lawyers called the verdict a great victory, while prosecutors and the judge treated the testimony of violence at the trial as relevant to what he deserved. Whether a judge may do that is now the question before the Second Circuit.

The indictment charged five counts, and Combs pleaded not guilty to all of them. Prosecutors said he led a criminal enterprise made up of some of his closest employees, which used threats and violence to force Ventura and a second woman, "Jane", to take part in drug-fuelled sexual performances with male sex workers, CNN reported. NPR explained that the racketeering charge was the hardest to follow. Prosecutors argued that Combs used a legitimate business empire, spanning music, clothing, alcohol and media, to fuel and hide crimes. The indictment listed kidnapping, arson, bribery, forced labour and coercing women among them.

The defence did not deny that Combs had been violent. Its lawyers acknowledged domestic violence but said the sexual performances, known as "freak offs", were consensual, and that the two women were strong, independent people who took part because they wanted to please him, Reuters reported. Combs's lawyers described the sexual encounters as preferences rather than crimes.

Ventura, a singer and model who was involved with Combs for more than a decade, was a central witness. NPR said she told jurors he raped and abused her, and that she felt forced to take part in the "freak offs" and could not safely leave. According to Reuters, both she and Jane told the court that he beat them, and that he threatened to cut off their financial support or leak sexually explicit images of them. Prosecutors also showed jurors a 2016 hotel surveillance video, aired by CNN in May 2024, in which Combs kicks and drags Ventura and throws a vase at her. The musician Scott Mescudi, known as Kid Cudi, told the court he believes Combs entered his home and was involved in the burning of his car, after Combs learned that Mescudi and Ventura had been seeing each other.

The prosecution called 34 witnesses, among them Dawn Richard, who was part of the group Danity Kane, according to CNN. Ventura had sued Combs in November 2023 for sex trafficking and settled a day later for $20 million, Reuters noted. Combs has denied all wrongdoing, Reuters noted.

The jury sent a note at 9:52 a.m. on 2 July saying it had reached verdicts on every count, after the judge had instructed it to keep working when it could not agree on one. The jury unanimously acquitted him of racketeering conspiracy and both sex trafficking counts, according to Reuters. On the two transportation counts it returned guilty verdicts. LawCommentary described those as arranging for male escorts to travel across state lines to take part in encounters with Combs's partners. The two counts carried up to 10 years each.

ABC7 pointed out that the jury's verdict meant that it did not find that Combs coerced or exploited his victims, which sex trafficking required, while it did find that he transported people across state lines for the "freak offs". Combs clapped and told family members "I'm gonna be home soon". Lawyer Marc Agnifilo called it "a great victory". Ventura's lawyer said she had "paved the way" for the convictions that did come.

The same afternoon the judge refused to release Combs on bail. Subramanian said it was impossible for the defendant to show by clear and convincing evidence that he posed no danger, and that Combs had shown a "disregard for the rule of law and a propensity of violence". Ventura's lawyers had written to the court arguing he was likely to pose a danger to the victims who testified. Prosecutors, Reuters reported, pointed to Jane's testimony that he assaulted her in June 2024, when he knew he was under investigation.

Before sentencing, prosecutors acknowledged in a court filing that the federal guidelines appeared to recommend at most about five and a quarter years, while Combs's lawyers argued that two years was the limit, Reuters reported. By the hearing on 3 October, the defence was asking for 14 months, and, according to Variety, prosecutors had raised their request from four or five years to 135 months. ABC7 said the prosecutors had initially asked for an 11-year sentence, which differs from Variety's account.

Combs spoke for longer at the hearing than at any point in the eight-week trial, Variety reported. He apologised to Ventura, to Jane and to others, called his actions "disgusting, shameful and sick" and said "I'll never put my hands on another person again". His six adult children spoke in his defence. Prosecutor Christy Slavik said he had not admitted his guilt or accepted responsibility.

The judge began by acknowledging Combs's career and philanthropy, then turned to the trial. "We saw the video of your savage beating of Ms. Ventura," he said, and he called the offences ones that "irreparably harmed two women". He imposed 50 months, a $500,000 fine and five years of supervised release. He told Combs that the same power he used to hurt women he could use to help them. In rejecting a shorter term, according to ABC7, the judge said a lengthy sentence was needed "to send a message to abusers and victims alike that exploitation and violence against women is met with real accountability".

The Second Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments on 9 April 2026. Combs's lawyers make two arguments. The first is that the sentence is unlawful because the judge counted conduct of which the jury had acquitted him. "He sits in prison today, serving a 50-month sentence, because the district judge acted as a thirteenth juror," his brief says. They also call the sentence four times the usual one for the offence. The second is that the conviction itself should fall, because they say the encounters were choreographed performances making "typical amateur pornography", conduct that they say the First Amendment protects.

The Manhattan US Attorney's Office replied that the guidelines allow a judge to consider relevant conduct, since "acquittal on criminal charges does not prove that the defendant is innocent". On the First Amendment, prosecutors said that transporting people to have sex for money is not inherently expressive, and that watching or filming the encounters would not shield a defendant from liability.

The panel of three judges, which included Judge William Nardini, did not rule from the bench and called the case "exceptionally difficult", according to LitigationLogic. LawCommentary reported that one judge asked why the court should disregard evidence from the trial, and a judge asked prosecutors why they should not be held to the way they presented the case, given that they had stressed the racketeering and trafficking charges and ended up relying on the Mann Act counts. If the court vacated the sentence, the case would go back to Subramanian for resentencing. LawCommentary also reported that Combs had reportedly written to President Donald Trump asking for a pardon, and said it was unclear whether the request would be considered.

Combs, now 56, was arrested in September 2024. ABC7 said he had spent about 14 months at the federal jail in Brooklyn before the trial and sentencing, and that time counts against his sentence, though Variety put the figure at 12 months at the time of sentencing. ABC7 said he may also be eligible for reductions under the First Step Act and for completing a drug rehabilitation programme.

The Bureau of Prisons' projected release date has moved repeatedly. It was April 2028 at the time of the appeal hearing and, WBLS reported in October 2026, had shifted to 21 January 2028. WBLS said that at one point the date had moved back to 20 February after a reported altercation with another inmate, after which Combs reportedly spent time in solitary confinement. The same report said that NBC News had reported allegations that Combs received special treatment from other inmates, that reports also alleged he had access to prohibited items, and that he had reportedly been returned to the prison's Special Housing Unit. The Bureau of Prisons has declined to discuss his housing, and Combs's representatives have pushed back against the reports. The Bureau does not explain the reason for each change in the date.
